headline: How a 1993 Rubber-Seal Theorem Explains the AI Capability Leap
lede: David Oks, a research partner at Andreessen Horowitz with an Oxford economics background, reached for a decades-old paper to explain something AI practitioners have felt but struggled to articulate: that frontier language models now seem to complete entire complex projects, not merely answer isolated questions. The mechanism is Nobel laureate Michael Kremer's *O-ring production function*, named after the Space Shuttle Challenger disaster. Projects are multiplicative chains of subtasks; small gains in per-task reliability compound into large gains in end-to-end success probability.
body:
In 1993, Kremer published “The O-Ring Theory of Economic Development” in the *Quarterly Journal of Economics*, modeling production as a **multiplicative chain**: each task must succeed, and total output is the product of per-task success probabilities rather than their sum. The name came from the 1986 Challenger disaster — the shuttle destroyed not because most of its systems failed, but because a single rubber seal did, erasing billions of dollars in value. A worker improving from 90% task reliability to 95% seems only modestly better; across a ten-task chain, that shift moves project-completion probability from roughly 35% to 60%. The richer the bundle, the larger the return to each marginal improvement.

Oks applies this directly to what frontier **large language models** can now do. A software project — building a web application, completing an *agentic workflow*, drafting a research document — is precisely such an O-ring bundle: it requires coherent code generation, correct API calls, edge-case handling, test writing, deployment configuration, and dozens of subsidiary steps. If a model previously failed one subtask in four, the probability of a clean end-to-end run was negligible. As reliability climbs toward one failure in ten, then one in twenty, the probability of threading the entire needle rises far faster than the underlying error rate falls. The subjective experience — “insane insane insane,” in Oks’s telling — is exactly what the multiplicative math predicts.

Independent measurement supports the intuition. METR, a model-evaluation nonprofit, tracks what it calls *task-completion time horizons* — the complexity of tasks, measured in hours of expert human effort, that frontier AI agents can reliably complete. Their data shows this metric doubling roughly every seven months since 2019. Andrej Karpathy called 2025 “the year AI crossed a capability threshold necessary to build all kinds of impressive programs simply via English”; Simon Willison documented models advancing from 30-minute tasks to multi-hour ones within a single calendar year.

The O-ring logic cuts both ways. The economist Josh Hendrickson has argued that the same multiplicative complementarity that amplifies skill gains inside a project also creates macroeconomic bottlenecks: if one input to the broader economy remains hard to automate, it becomes the binding constraint on aggregate output even as other tasks approach zero cost. Oks’s observation is deliberately scoped to the project level — within a given bundle of tasks, linear gains in model ability compound into superlinear gains in success rate — and does not make the stronger claim that GDP growth will track the same exponential curve.

concepts.definition: A model of production developed by economist Michael Kremer in 1993 in which total output equals the product, not the sum, of each task’s quality level. Named after the Challenger disaster, where a single failed rubber seal destroyed the whole mission. The implication is that small improvements in any component compound multiplicatively across the whole project, so high-skill inputs cluster together and the weakest link dominates.

AI systems trained on vast text corpora to predict and generate language. Frontier examples include GPT-4o, Claude, and Gemini. At sufficient scale they exhibit emergent reasoning and code-generation capabilities used as the backbone of modern AI agents and coding assistants.

A metric developed by METR (Model Evaluation and Threat Research) measuring the longest task — in hours of equivalent expert human effort — that a frontier AI agent can reliably complete. It is used to track the expanding scope of AI autonomous capability over time and has been doubling roughly every seven months since 2019 according to METR’s own data.

A multi-step task in which an AI model takes a sequence of actions — running code, searching the web, writing files, calling APIs — with minimal human intervention between steps. The AI acts as an “agent” pursuing a goal rather than a simple question-answerer responding to a single prompt.

A production structure in which component qualities are multiplied together rather than added. A chain of ten tasks each at 90% reliability yields only about a 35% chance of overall success; raising each to 95% lifts that to roughly 60%. This non-linearity is the core mechanism behind the O-ring production function.
